newsitem.title: UK: UK to open up digital TV access on "fair" terms.
newsitem.headline: UK to open up digital TV access on "fair" terms.

text.p: Britain pledged on Wednesday to only licence access technology for digital television on what it called "fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory" terms.

Industry watchdog Don Cruickshank told a news conference that it was too soon to define licence terms. But he said he would deny the first market player a monopoly position, while allowing it a reasonable rate of return.
Pay television in Britain, in which British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc is the dominant player, is currently subscription based.
But the move to digital technology with hundreds of extra channels will pave the way for specific pay-per-view events, such as soccer matches and hollywood blockbusters.

In an attempt to draw a balance between encouraging investment in digital access technology and preventing anti- competitive practices, Cruickshank said there would be an open consultation in December and the first few months of 1997 on how to enforce a licence.
Conditional access technology, or "set-top-boxes", support pay television. Signals are scrambled and consumers can only watch chosen programmes by paying to have them unscrambled.
Cruickshank said consumers should be able get "hassle free access" to requested programmes at an affordable price and with the proper technical support and standards.
At the same time all broadcasters should be able to gain access on reasonable and fair terms to any digital set top boxes which can receive their signals.

BSkyB is launching digital satellite services late next year, while digital terrestrial television is not expected to begin broadcasting until mid 1998. The Department of Trade and Industry said it would try to prevent manufacturers of set to boxes from favouring one system over the other.
"Our objective is to foster the development of a competitive market in digital services on all means of delivery," minister for science and technology Ian Taylor told reporters.
"This means that it is important that innovations and early investment should be rewarded and not over-regulated.

"At the same time we have sought to provide strong safeguards that will allow the regulator to act quickly and firmly in dealing with any anti-competitive abuse of any advantage gained by moving first into the market."

A short, final round of consultation and comments are invited by December 11. Regulations should be available to Parliament before the parliamentary recess and subject to approval, come into force withing 21 calendar days, he added.
